title: NSCA’s Essentials of Sport Science
authors: Duncan N. French and Lorena Torres Ronda, editors; individual chapter authors identified in locators
population: Multiple sports and athlete levels; examples require translation to baseball.
access: Paid textbook. Cited by chapter and page; no text, tables or figures are reproduced.
findings: Provides frameworks for needs analysis, planning, load measurement, force–velocity assessment, measurement error, and interdisciplinary interpretation.
limitations: Foundational synthesis rather than a baseball intervention trial. Some examples concern soccer or individual sports. Historical workload theories are not adopted as validated safety rules.
locations: Chapter 1, Performance Dimensions (Winkelman & Norman), pp. 75–81 and 86–89: interdisciplinary roles, interpretation and decisions.
Chapter 2, Training Load Model (Cormack & Coutts), pp. 94–96 and 118–122: dose–response, monitoring components and statistical issues.
Chapter 3, Periodization and Programming for Individual Sports (Haff), pp. 132–133 and 145–155: planning versus programming, microcycles, schedule constraints.
Chapter 4, Periodization and Programming for Team Sports (Buchheit & Laursen), pp. 164–169: physiological objectives and integration of conditioning.
Chapter 6, Profiling and Benchmarking (McGuigan), pp. 235–240: analysis of athlete, norms and benchmarking.
Chapter 8, Data Hygiene (Varley, Lovell & Carey), pp. 292–302: validity, reliability and meaningful change.
Chapter 11, Kinematics and Gait Analysis (King & Richter), pp. 397–398: reliability, SEM and minimal detectable change.

title: Offseason Workout Recommendations for Baseball Players
authors: Brooks Klein, Daniel Cobian, Goldy Simmons, Michael Reinold
population: Baseball training, with a professional/minor-league offseason example and supporting studies from mixed populations.
access: Free full text verified on PMC.
findings: Discusses multidirectional strength/power and a progression from recovery through preparation to baseball-specific work.
limitations: Sample programming is illustrative, not an experimentally established optimal plan. Several exercise restrictions and mechanistic claims should be treated as author recommendations rather than universal rules.
locations: Unique Training Demands of Baseball.
Principles of Strength and Conditioning in Baseball Players: Functional Assessments, Develop Strength, Maximize Power.
Overview of Offseason Programming: Factors and Considerations; Tables 1–2.
license: Copyright authors under exclusive Springer licence. Link and concise original summary only; figures and program tables not reproduced.

title: Biomechanical and Neuromuscular Performance Requirements of Horizontal Deceleration: A Review with Implications for Random Intermittent Multi-Directional Sports
authors: Damian J. Harper, Alistair J. McBurnie, Thomas Dos’Santos, Ola Eriksrud, Martin Evans, Daniel D. Cohen, David Rhodes, Christopher Carling, John Kiely
population: Multidirectional sport participants; many studies use planned tasks in soccer and other non-baseball populations.
access: Open full text verified at the publisher.
findings: Braking requires both control of momentum and attenuation of force; strength qualities and coordination contribute.
limitations: Most evidence is not baseball-specific. Planned stopping tasks do not establish injury prevention or game agility outcomes.
locations: Section 3: Biomechanical Demands of Horizontal Deceleration.
Section 4.1: Technical Ability.
Section 5: Neuromuscular Performance Determinants of Horizontal Deceleration.

title: Reliability and Test-Retest Agreement of Mechanical Variables Obtained During Countermovement Jump
authors: Alisson A. Souza, Martim Bottaro, Valdinar A. Rocha Junior, Victor Lage, James J. Tufano, Amilton Vieira
population: 41 physically active men, mean age approximately 24; not a professional-baseball sample.
access: Free journal PDF verified, 12 PDF pages; journal pagination 6–17.
findings: Reliability varied by metric. RFD had more relative error than peak force in this protocol. A high ICC alone did not establish low absolute error.
limitations: Single rater and specified equipment, calculation methods and trial aggregation. Reported coefficients cannot be transplanted as local baseball thresholds.
locations: Methods: Participants and Protocol, printed pp. 7–9 (pp. 2–4).
Results and Table 1, printed p. 10 (p. 5).
Discussion, printed pp. 10–13 (pp. 5–8), especially ICC dependence on sample variability and study limitations.
license: Public PDF access verified; redistribution terms not established from reviewed PDF. Link and concise original summary only.

title: Unaccounted Workload Factor: Game-Day Pitch Counts in High School Baseball Pitchers—An Observational Study
authors: Jason L. Zaremski, Giorgio Zeppieri Jr, Deborah L. Jones, Brady L. Tripp, Michelle Bruner, Heather K. Vincent, MaryBeth Horodyski
population: 115 varsity high-school starting-pitcher outings across 34 North Central Florida schools during 2017.
access: Free full-text PDF verified at the authors’ university.
findings: Bullpen and between-inning pitches comprised a substantial portion of counted mound throws outside official game totals.
limitations: Observational exposure counts; did not test an injury association, measure tissue load or establish professional recovery thresholds.
locations: Abstract and Methods, PDF/printed pp. 1–2.
Results, PDF/printed pp. 2–3.
Limitations, PDF/printed p. 5.

population: Professional pitchers and position players; practitioner programming examples.

population: General athletic populations; original baseball applications are explicitly illustrative

findings: Supports mechanical definitions, neural contributions to force, overlapping energy pathways, task-specific sprint and agility distinctions, stretch–shortening concepts, and task-oriented warm-up and mobility reasoning.
limitations: Textbook synthesis, not a baseball intervention trial. Historical simplifications and categorical efficacy statements are not adopted.
